title: The Café
strapline: Table for two? Menus, orders and very carefully carried trays.
intent: The café bundles together the best of social life: welcoming customers, taking orders, serving food and sitting down together to eat and chat.
Waiter-and-customer talk is naturally polite and naturally turn-taking — 'what would you like?', 'anything else?', 'enjoy your meal'.
Order pads give mark-making an urgent, genuine purpose — the kitchen needs to know what table three wants.
Menus, specials boards and the open sign put print to work where children can't miss it.
Pouring drinks, balancing loaded trays and setting tables are precise physical work with real consequences for getting it wrong.
Matching cups to customers, counting out the right number of plates and 'adding up the bill' keep number honest and useful.
implementation: Be a demanding-but-kind customer: change your order, ask what the waiter recommends, query the bill — every problem extends the talk.
Model the service script until it becomes the children's own: 'Are you ready to order?', 'Coming right up!', 'Was everything alright for you?'
Make menus with the children — photos, drawings and words of real dishes, including foods from their own homes.
Keep order pads and pencils clipped to every waiter's apron, and treat every order slip as a real message to the kitchen.
Let children pour real water from small jugs and carry real (unbreakable) crockery — trust builds control.
Slip maths into service: 'Table two wants three teas — how many cups do you need?', 'That's two pounds for the cake and one for the juice.'
Visit a real café for a babyccino and watch what the children carry back into their play.
key_questions: What would you like to order today — and how will you remember it?
What's on the menu? What do you recommend?
Table four wants four teas — how many cups do you need on the tray?
How will you carry it all without spilling?
What shall we put on the specials board today?

impact.text: Children sustain café storylines with shared roles — chef, waiter, customer — negotiating who does what and keeping the service running.
Children 'write' orders on their pads and deliver them to the kitchen, telling the chef exactly what each mark says.
Children use the menu and specials board as working print — pointing to dishes, spotting familiar words and photos.
Children pour drinks from jugs and carry loaded trays with growing precision and patience.
Children count out the right number of cups, plates and spoons for each table, matching one to each customer.
Waiter and customer hold genuine polite conversations across several turns — ordering, recommending, checking everything was alright.
Children talk about foods they've tried and what different people like to eat, drawing on tastes from many kitchens.

enhancements: Real small jugs, teapots and unbreakable cups so the pouring is genuinely wet.
Aprons with a pocket for the order pad and pencil.
A photographic menu made with the children, featuring dishes from their own family tables.
A specials board and chalk to change what's cooking each day.
Playdough cakes and pastries for the counter display, priced with little tickets.
A bell for 'order up!' between kitchen and floor.
A real trip to a local café — order, pay and come home with new storylines.

playing_exploring: Children step into a busy grown-up world they've sat and watched from a highchair.
The props pull children in — a teapot demands pouring, an order pad demands writing.
active_learning: An order taken must be cooked, carried and served: children hold a multi-step sequence in mind and see it through.
creating_thinking: Children invent dishes, daily specials and solutions — what do we do when two tables want the last slice of cake?
